## Guide: Foreign MSB registration in Canada

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/foreign-msb-registration-canada.html

A business with no office in Canada may still have to register with FINTRAC. It does if it directs and provides money services to people or entities in Canada.

**Key points:**
- Foreign MSBs that direct and provide services to Canada must register first.
- Marketing to Canadians, a .ca domain or Canadian listings can count.
- You need a representative for service who lives in Canada.
- The foreign business stays responsible for its obligations.

### What is a foreign MSB?

A foreign money services business (FMSB) has no place of business in Canada but directs and provides money services to people or entities in Canada. The money services are the same ones that apply to Canadian MSBs:

- foreign exchange dealing;

- remitting or transmitting funds;

- issuing or redeeming money orders, traveller's cheques or similar negotiable instruments;

- dealing in virtual currency;

- crowdfunding platform services;

- armoured car services;

- cheque cashing;

- acquirer services for private automated banking machines.

A foreign MSB must register with FINTRAC before it starts providing these services to Canada. A business with a place of business in Canada, such as a physical location, is a domestic MSB under [FINTRAC's definitions](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/msb-eng), and registers as one. Our [guide to registering an MSB](https://amlcanada.ca/how-to-register-msb-canada.html) covers the steps for both.

### What counts as directing services at Canada

FINTRAC looks at whether your business targets people in Canada. Examples it gives include marketing aimed at people in Canada, operating a .ca domain name, and being listed in a Canadian business directory. If your website, ads or partnerships are built to attract Canadian customers, assume you're in scope and get it confirmed.

### Your representative for service in Canada

A foreign MSB must name a representative for service who resides in Canada and is authorized to accept notices from FINTRAC on its behalf. The representative doesn't take over your obligations. The foreign business itself stays responsible for complying with Canada's anti-money laundering law.

If the representative's name or address for service changes, you must tell FINTRAC within 30 days. If you don't, FINTRAC must deny the application or revoke the registration ([PCMLTFA subsection 11.13(2)](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html)).

The representative is a person. Having a Canadian business address is a separate matter from the representative requirement. Some foreign MSBs want one for banking, partners or customers. We offer a [Canadian business address](https://amlcanada.ca/canadian-address.html), and you can ask us about the representative requirement in your consultation.

### Obligations once registered

Foreign MSBs carry substantially the same obligations as Canadian ones: a compliance program, client identification, record keeping, reporting to FINTRAC, the travel rule for funds and virtual currency transfers, and renewing their registration every two years, with changes reported within 30 days. Our [FINTRAC reporting guide](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-reporting-requirements.html) sets out which reports apply.

Many foreign MSBs don't have an experienced compliance person in Canada. Some appoint an [outsourced compliance officer](https://amlcanada.ca/outsourced-compliance-officer.html) who works with FINTRAC's requirements.

### Criminal record checks from abroad

FINTRAC needs criminal record checks for the CEO, president, directors and anyone owning or controlling 20% or more, issued in each person's country of residence within six months before you apply. Checks that aren't in English or French need a translation attested by a certified translator. For international ownership, this is usually the longest step.

### Questions

**Do foreign companies need to register with FINTRAC?** Yes, if they direct and provide money services to people or entities in Canada. They register as foreign MSBs before they start.

**Does a foreign MSB need a Canadian address?** FINTRAC requires a representative for service who resides in Canada. A Canadian business address is a separate thing that some foreign MSBs also want for banking, partners and customers.

**What if our representative for service changes?** Tell FINTRAC within 30 days. If the new name or address isn't provided in time, FINTRAC must deny the application or revoke the registration.

**Can a foreign MSB outsource its compliance officer?** Many do. The foreign business stays responsible for its obligations, but an experienced compliance officer in Canada can carry the day-to-day work.

Sources: [FINTRAC, Money services businesses](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/msb-eng); [Register your MSB or FMSB](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/register-inscrire/reg-ins-eng); [Travel rule](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/travel-acheminement/1-eng); [Update, renew or cancel your registration](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/register-inscrire/respond-eng); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html). Checked 11 October 2026.

---

## Guide: FINTRAC reporting for MSBs: which report, and when

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-reporting-requirements.html

Money services businesses report suspicious transactions, large cash, international transfers, large virtual currency receipts and listed person property to FINTRAC. Each report has its own trigger and deadline.

**Key points:**
- STRs have no minimum amount and are due as soon as practicable.
- LCTR, EFTR and LVCTR apply at $10,000 or more.
- The 24-hour rule adds up transactions you know are linked.
- Threshold reports are due within 5 working days to 15 calendar days.

### The reports at a glance

| Report | When it applies | Deadline |

| Suspicious transaction report (STR) | Reasonable grounds to suspect a transaction is related to money laundering, terrorist financing or, since August 19, 2024, sanctions evasion. No minimum amount. | As soon as practicable |

| Large cash transaction report (LCTR) | Cash of $10,000 or more, in one transaction or in two or more that the 24-hour rule requires you to add together. | 15 calendar days |

| Electronic funds transfer report (EFTR) | International electronic funds transfers of $10,000 or more, in one transfer or in two or more that the 24-hour rule requires you to add together. | 5 working days |

| Large virtual currency transaction report (LVCTR) | Virtual currency worth $10,000 or more, in one transaction or in two or more that the 24-hour rule requires you to add together. | 5 working days |

| Listed person or entity property report | Property you know or believe is owned or controlled by a terrorist group or a listed person or entity. Since October 1, 2025, this includes persons listed under the Special Economic Measures Act and the Sergei Magnitsky Law. Called the terrorist property report until March 2, 2025. You must also disclose the property to the RCMP and CSIS without delay. | Immediately |

Amounts are in Canadian dollars, or the equivalent in another currency or in virtual currency.

### Suspicious transaction reports (STR)

You must report a transaction, or an attempted one, when you have reasonable grounds to suspect it's related to money laundering, terrorist financing or, since August 19, 2024, a sanctions evasion offence ([PCMLTFA section 7](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html)). A sanctions evasion offence means breaching a sanctions restriction under the United Nations Act, the Special Economic Measures Act or the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act. [FINTRAC's sanctions evasion guidance](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/sanctions/sanctions-eng) explains how to flag these reports, and its [August 2024 notice](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/notices-avis/avs/2024-08-02-eng) announced the change.

There's no minimum amount. FINTRAC expects the report "as soon as practicable": somewhere between immediately and as soon as possible, with completing the STR taking priority over other tasks.

Good STRs explain why: what you saw, the indicators, and how the facts fit together. A transaction can need both an STR and another report, for example a suspicious large cash deposit.

### Large cash transaction reports (LCTR)

When you receive $10,000 or more in cash, in one transaction or in several that the 24-hour rule adds together, you report it within 15 calendar days. See [FINTRAC's LCTR guidance](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/lctr-doie/lctr-doie-eng).

### Electronic funds transfer reports (EFTR)

International electronic funds transfers of $10,000 or more, sent or finally received, in one transfer or in several that the 24-hour rule adds together, are reported within 5 working days.

### Large virtual currency transaction reports (LVCTR)

When you receive virtual currency worth $10,000 or more, in one transaction or in several that the 24-hour rule adds together, you report it within 5 working days after the day you receive it. A working day is Monday to Friday, excluding public holidays.

### The 24-hour rule

The 24-hour rule stops threshold reporting being avoided by splitting transactions. When you know that two or more transactions of the same type, totalling $10,000 or more within a 24-hour window, were conducted by the same person or entity, on behalf of the same person or entity, or for the same beneficiary, you report them together. The individual transactions can be any amount.

FINTRAC uses a static 24-hour window: you set fixed 24-hour periods, for example 9 a.m. one day to 8:59 a.m. the next. If a client gives you $6,000 in cash at 10 a.m. and another $5,000 at 3 p.m. in the same window, you file one LCTR for $11,000. Your systems need to add these up. [FINTRAC's 24-hour rule guidance](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/24hour/1-eng) has more examples.

### Listed person or entity property reports

If you know or believe property in your possession or control is owned or controlled by a listed person or entity, you must file a Listed Person or Entity Property Report with FINTRAC immediately, and you can't deal with that property. This report replaced the terrorist property report on March 2, 2025. Since October 1, 2025, it also covers persons and entities listed under the Special Economic Measures Act and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act.

Separately from the FINTRAC report, the law requires you to disclose the property without delay to the Commissioner of the RCMP and the Director of CSIS. See [FINTRAC's listed person property guidance](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/Guide5/5-eng).

### The travel rule

When MSBs send electronic funds or virtual currency transfers, the information about who requested the transfer and the beneficiary must travel with it: names, addresses and account or reference numbers. Received travel-rule information can't be stripped out. The travel rule doesn't involve filing a report. It supports your record keeping and reporting.

### Getting reporting right

- Know which reports apply to your services, and test that your systems flag them.

- Track deadlines from the right day, in working days or calendar days as the report requires.

- Document why you did or didn't file an STR.

- Keep the records behind every report, generally for at least five years.

Your [policies and procedures](https://amlcanada.ca/compliance-programs.html) should set out how each of these is done, and staff who handle transactions need [training](https://amlcanada.ca/training.html) on them. An [outsourced compliance officer](https://amlcanada.ca/outsourced-compliance-officer.html) can handle this reporting.

### Questions

**What is the FINTRAC reporting threshold?** $10,000 for large cash, international electronic funds transfer and large virtual currency transaction reports, including linked transactions that add up to $10,000 within 24 hours. Suspicious transaction reports have no threshold.

**How long do I have to file an EFTR?** 5 working days.

**How long do I have to file an LCTR?** 15 calendar days after the day you receive the cash.

**When is an STR due?** As soon as practicable, which FINTRAC describes as between immediately and as soon as possible.

**Do I report suspected sanctions evasion to FINTRAC?** Yes. Since August 19, 2024, suspicious transaction reports also cover transactions you have reasonable grounds to suspect are related to a sanctions evasion offence.

Sources: [FINTRAC, Reporting suspicious transactions](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/str-dod/str-dod-eng); [Report suspected sanctions evasion](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/sanctions/sanctions-eng); [FINTRAC notice, August 2, 2024](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/notices-avis/avs/2024-08-02-eng); [Reporting large cash transactions](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/lctr-doie/lctr-doie-eng); [Reporting electronic funds transfers](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/eft-dt/eft-dt-eng); [Reporting large virtual currency transactions](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/lvctr/lvctr-eng); [The 24-hour rule](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/24hour/1-eng); [Reporting listed person or entity property](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/Guide5/5-eng); [Travel rule](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/travel-acheminement/1-eng); [Record keeping for MSBs](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/recordkeeping-document/record/msb-eng); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html). Checked 11 October 2026.

---

## Guide: What is the RPAA?

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-registration-guide.html

The Retail Payment Activities Act is the federal law under which the Bank of Canada supervises payment service providers. It sets rules on operational risk, incidents and the safeguarding of users' funds.

**Key points:**
- The RPAA applies to payment service providers performing retail payment activities.
- Foreign PSPs are covered when they direct activities at Canada and serve end users here.
- Banks, credit unions and some other institutions are excluded.
- The RPAA sits alongside FINTRAC rules, and many businesses need both.

### What the RPAA is

The [Retail Payment Activities Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/R-7.36/FullText.html) (RPAA) brought payment service providers (PSPs) under federal supervision for the first time. Payment processors, digital wallets and money transfer apps are typical examples. The Bank of Canada supervises them, with a focus on three things: managing operational risk, responding to incidents, and protecting the funds PSPs hold for their users.

The Act defines a PSP as an individual or entity that performs payment functions as a service or business activity that isn't incidental to another service or business activity. A retail payment activity is a payment function performed in relation to an electronic funds transfer in Canadian or another currency.

### The five payment functions

The Act lists five payment functions. A PSP performs one or more of them for end users:

- keeping an account for one or more end users that's used for electronic funds transfers;

- holding funds for an end user until they're withdrawn or sent to someone else;

- starting an electronic funds transfer when an end user asks for it;

- authorizing an electronic funds transfer, or transmitting, receiving or facilitating the instruction for one;

- clearing or settlement services.

### Who the Act covers

The RPAA applies to retail payment activities performed by a PSP with a place of business in Canada. It also applies to a PSP outside Canada that directs retail payment activities at individuals or entities in Canada and performs them for end users in Canada (RPAA section 5).

A new PSP must register with the Bank before it performs any retail payment activities, according to the [Bank's registration criteria](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/06/criteria-for-registering-payment-service-providers/). Registered PSPs are listed on the Bank's public registry.

### What's excluded

Sections 6 to 10 of the Act set out exclusions. Some institutions are outside the RPAA, including banks, authorized foreign banks, provincially regulated credit unions and caisses populaires, insurance companies, federal trust and loan companies, and provincially regulated trust companies.

Some activities are excluded too, including payments made with closed-loop instruments such as gift cards that can be used only with the issuing merchant or a group of merchants, cash withdrawals at ATMs, and certain securities and financial contract transactions. An agent of a registered PSP that is acting within its authority and is on the PSP's list of agents isn't separately covered.

### Registration, review and fees

The Bank charges a one-time, non-refundable application fee. It was CA$2,500 when registration opened in November 2024, and it's set by [regulation](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2023-229/FullText.html) and adjusted for inflation each January. We confirm the current amount before you apply. The Bank plans to charge registered PSPs annual assessment fees to recover the cost of supervision, but it hasn't started yet. Its [FAQ](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/08/frequently-asked-questions-about-retail-payments-supervision/) says it will begin charging them in due course, once the fee formula is finalized.

Application information is shared with the Department of Finance and with FINTRAC. If the Minister of Finance considers it necessary for national security reasons, the Minister can order a full review of an application, and the Bank can't register the applicant while that review is under way. Our [RPAA registration service](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-registration.html) covers the application itself.

### Ongoing obligations

Since September 8, 2025, PSPs must have a risk management and incident response framework, and those that hold end-user funds must safeguard them, either in a trust account or in a segregated account with insurance or a guarantee.

When a PSP becomes aware of an incident with a material impact, it must notify the Bank and the affected end users, PSPs or clearing houses without delay (RPAA section 18). The Bank's [reporting reminder](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/06/reminder-psp-reporting-obligations-under-rpaa/) says the initial notice to the Bank is due no later than 48 hours after the PSP determines the incident is material. PSPs also give notice at least five business days before a significant change or new activity, and file an annual report by March 31. Our [RPAA compliance program](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-compliance-program.html) covers these frameworks.

### RPAA and FINTRAC

The two regimes sit side by side. The RPAA deals with operational risk and safeguarding under the Bank of Canada. FINTRAC deals with money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions evasion under the PCMLTFA. A payment business that also remits or transmits funds usually needs to [register with FINTRAC as an MSB](https://amlcanada.ca/how-to-register-msb-canada.html) as well as with the Bank.

### Questions

**What does RPAA stand for?** The Retail Payment Activities Act, the law under which the Bank of Canada supervises payment service providers.

**How much is the Bank of Canada's RPAA fee?** A one-time, non-refundable application fee. It was CA$2,500 when introduced in November 2024 and is adjusted for inflation each January, so we confirm the current amount before you apply. Annual assessment fees aren't charged yet.

**Do foreign PSPs have to register under the RPAA?** Yes, if they direct retail payment activities at individuals or entities in Canada and perform them for end users in Canada.

**When does a PSP have to notify the Bank of an incident?** Without delay, and no later than 48 hours after it determines that the incident has a material impact. Affected end users, PSPs and clearing houses must also be notified.

**How long does RPAA registration take?** In our experience, generally about 2 to 8 months, including the national security review.

Sources: [Retail Payment Activities Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/R-7.36/FullText.html); [Retail Payment Activities Regulations](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2023-229/FullText.html); [Bank of Canada, Retail payments supervision](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/regulatory-oversight/retail-payments/); [Supervisory framework](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/regulatory-oversight/retail-payments/supervisory-framework/); [Retail payments supervision FAQ](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/08/frequently-asked-questions-about-retail-payments-supervision/); [Registration application fee](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/10/registration-application-fee/); [Criteria for registering PSPs](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/06/criteria-for-registering-payment-service-providers/); [PSP reporting obligations](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/06/reminder-psp-reporting-obligations-under-rpaa/). Checked 11 October 2026.

## Guide: Registering a crypto business with FINTRAC

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/crypto-registration-canada.html

Crypto exchanges and virtual currency dealers register with FINTRAC as money services businesses, whether they're based in Canada or serve Canadians from abroad.

**Key points:**
- Dealing in virtual currency is a money service: register with FINTRAC first.
- Foreign crypto businesses serving Canada register as foreign MSBs.
- Report virtual currency receipts of $10,000+ within 5 working days.
- Trading platforms also deal with provincial securities regulators.

### Crypto businesses register as MSBs

Dealing in virtual currency is one of the money services FINTRAC lists, so crypto exchanges and virtual currency dealers register with FINTRAC as money services businesses before they start. A crypto business outside Canada that directs and provides these services to people in Canada registers as a [foreign MSB](https://amlcanada.ca/foreign-msb-registration-canada.html). The [registration steps](https://amlcanada.ca/how-to-register-msb-canada.html) are the same as for any MSB.

### Large virtual currency transaction reports

When you receive virtual currency worth $10,000 or more, you file a large virtual currency transaction report (LVCTR) within 5 working days after the day you receive it. Under the 24-hour rule, this includes several receipts within a 24-hour window that total $10,000 or more, when you know they were made by or for the same person or entity, or for the same beneficiary. See [FINTRAC's LVCTR guidance](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/lvctr/lvctr-eng). Suspicious transaction reports apply too, with no minimum amount. Our [FINTRAC reporting guide](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-reporting-requirements.html) covers both.

### The travel rule for virtual currency

When you send a virtual currency transfer, you must include the requester's name, address and account or reference number, and the beneficiary's name, address and account or reference number. When you receive transfers, you must take reasonable measures to make sure that information is included. You can't strip received travel-rule information out of a transfer.

### Record keeping

For virtual currency transfers of $1,000 or more, MSBs keep detailed records, including the date, the type and amount of virtual currency, client and beneficiary details, transaction hashes, sending and receiving addresses, and the exchange rates used. Records are generally kept for at least five years.

### Provincial rules

FINTRAC registration is federal. Crypto trading platforms are also regulated by provincial securities regulators. A platform operating in Canada is expected to register with them or, while it seeks registration, file a pre-registration undertaking, under [CSA Staff Notice 21-332](https://www.osc.ca/en/securities-law/instruments-rules-policies/2/21-332/csa-staff-notice-21-332-crypto-asset-trading-platforms-pre-registration-undertakings-changes). Platforms that let clients trade stablecoins, which securities regulators call value-referenced crypto assets, are expected to follow the terms in [CSA Staff Notice 21-333](https://www.osc.ca/en/securities-law/instruments-rules-policies/2/21-333/csa-staff-notice-21-333-crypto-asset-trading-platforms-terms-and-conditions-trading-value).

Quebec also licenses money-services businesses through Revenu Québec. We'll tell you when you need separate advice on these rules.

### Changes in 2025 and 2026

Since October 1, 2025, regulations strengthening the MSB registration framework have been in force, including obligations when MSBs engage agents or mandataries.

Bill C-12, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, raised the maximum administrative monetary penalty for violations after that date to $4 million per violation for a person and $20 million for an entity. It also requires compliance agreements after penalties, adds compliance orders, and requires compliance programs to be reasonably designed, risk-based and effective. FINTRAC lists these on its [changes page](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/businesses-entreprises/changes-changements-eng).

The Budget 2025 Implementation Act, which also received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, created the Stablecoin Act. It isn't in force yet. Under the [federal stablecoin framework](https://www.canada.ca/en/department-finance/programs/financial-sector-policy/canadas-stablecoin-framework.html), stablecoin issuers will register with the Bank of Canada, which will supervise them, and FINTRAC says they will also register with it as MSBs dealing in virtual currency.

### Your compliance program

A crypto MSB needs the same five-part compliance program as any MSB, written for crypto risks: wallet screening, blockchain analytics, travel rule handling and virtual currency reporting. Our [14-document program](https://amlcanada.ca/compliance-programs.html) includes a Travel Rule Policy and Procedure.

### Questions

**Do crypto exchanges need to register in Canada?** Yes. Dealing in virtual currency is a money service, so crypto exchanges and dealers register with FINTRAC as MSBs. Trading platforms also deal with provincial securities regulators.

**What is an LVCTR?** A large virtual currency transaction report, filed within 5 working days when you receive virtual currency worth $10,000 or more, including linked receipts that the 24-hour rule adds together.

**Does the travel rule apply to crypto in Canada?** Yes. MSBs must include requester and beneficiary information when they send virtual currency transfers, and take reasonable measures to check it's included when they receive them.

**Is the Stablecoin Act in force?** Not yet. It received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, and will come into force once its regulations are made.

Sources: [FINTRAC, Money services businesses](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/msb-eng); [Reporting large virtual currency transactions](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/lvctr/lvctr-eng); [The 24-hour rule](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/24hour/1-eng); [Travel rule](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/travel-acheminement/1-eng); [Record keeping for MSBs](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/recordkeeping-document/record/msb-eng); [FINTRAC, Changes to legislation and regulations](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/businesses-entreprises/changes-changements-eng); [Administrative monetary penalties: changes](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/pen/3-eng); [Department of Finance, Canada's stablecoin framework](https://www.canada.ca/en/department-finance/programs/financial-sector-policy/canadas-stablecoin-framework.html); [CSA Staff Notice 21-332](https://www.osc.ca/en/securities-law/instruments-rules-policies/2/21-332/csa-staff-notice-21-332-crypto-asset-trading-platforms-pre-registration-undertakings-changes); [CSA Staff Notice 21-333](https://www.osc.ca/en/securities-law/instruments-rules-policies/2/21-333/csa-staff-notice-21-333-crypto-asset-trading-platforms-terms-and-conditions-trading-value); [Revenu Québec, Money-services business licence](https://www.revenuquebec.ca/en/businesses/sector-specific-measures/money-services-businesses-msbs/money-services-business-licence-application/). Checked 11 October 2026.

## Guide: The two-year effectiveness review: a checklist

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-effectiveness-review-checklist.html

FINTRAC requires every reporting entity to review its compliance program at least every two years. The review should test how the program works in practice as well as what's written down.

**Key points:**
- Review every part of your compliance program at least every two years.
- An internal or external auditor does it, or you, if you have no auditor.
- If you're an entity, report the findings to a senior officer within 30 days.
- Test whether procedures are followed, as well as whether documents exist.

### What FINTRAC requires

Every business FINTRAC regulates must institute and document a plan to review the effectiveness of its compliance program, and carry out the review at least every two years. The plan must include all the elements of the program: policies and procedures, risk assessment and training. The requirements are in [FINTRAC's compliance program guidance](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/compliance-conformite/Guide4/4-eng).

The review is done by an internal or external auditor or, if you don't have an auditor, by yourself. FINTRAC's best-practice advice is that whoever does it shouldn't be directly involved in the compliance program activities being reviewed, so the review stays impartial. Some businesses use an [external effectiveness review](https://amlcanada.ca/effectiveness-reviews.html) for that reason.

### The checklist

### Policies and procedures

- Are they written, current, and approved by a senior officer (if you're an entity)?

- Do they reflect the services you offer today, including anything launched since the last review?

- Do they cover identification, beneficial ownership, politically exposed persons, third-party determination, ongoing monitoring, record keeping, reporting, ministerial directives and the travel rule where it applies?

### Risk assessment

- Does it cover your clients and business relationships, products, services and delivery channels, geography, and new developments and technologies?

- Does it assess sanctions evasion risk alongside money laundering and terrorist financing risk?

- Does it take account of the risks the latest National Risk Assessment identifies for your sector?

- Has it been updated for new products, markets or agents?

- Do your controls follow from it, with enhanced measures for high risk?

### Training

- Is there a written, [ongoing training program](https://amlcanada.ca/training.html) and plan?

- Did the people who need training, including agents, receive it, and are there records?

- Does the content match your risks and your staff's roles?

### The program in practice

- Sample client files: was identity verified the way your procedures say?

- Sample transactions: were reportable transactions reported on time, including under the 24-hour rule?

- Review unusual-activity decisions: were STR decisions documented either way?

- Check that records can be produced, and are kept for the required period.

- Check that findings from the last review were fixed.

If your policies or risk assessment need rewriting after the review, our [compliance program documents](https://amlcanada.ca/compliance-programs.html) can replace them.

### Reporting the results

If you're an entity, you must report in writing to a senior officer no later than 30 days after the review is completed. The report covers the findings of the review, the updates made to your policies and procedures during the reporting period, and the status of putting those updates in place. Keep the report. It's one of the first things an examiner may ask for, as our [examination guide](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-examination-preparation.html) explains.

### Common gaps

- A review that checks documents exist but never tests whether they're followed.

- The same review copied from the previous cycle.

- A risk assessment that hasn't changed since launch, though the business has.

- No assessment of sanctions evasion risk.

- Findings from the last review still open.

- No written report to a senior officer, or one sent late.

### Questions

**How often is an AML effectiveness review required?** At least every two years.

**Who can do the effectiveness review?** An internal or external auditor, or yourself if you don't have an auditor. FINTRAC suggests it shouldn't be someone directly involved in the activities being reviewed.

**What happens after the review?** If you're an entity, report the findings in writing to a senior officer within 30 days, along with the updates made to policies and procedures and how far they've been put in place.

Sources: [FINTRAC, Compliance program requirements](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/compliance-conformite/Guide4/4-eng); [Risk assessment guidance](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/compliance-conformite/rba/rba-eng); [The 24-hour rule](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/24hour/1-eng); [Report suspected sanctions evasion](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/transaction-operation/sanctions/sanctions-eng). Checked 11 October 2026.

---

## Guide: Preparing for a FINTRAC examination

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-examination-preparation.html

A FINTRAC examination usually starts with a call to your compliance officer and a letter asking for documents. Examinations can be done remotely or on site, and findings can lead to follow-up or a penalty.

**Key points:**
- The examination starts on the date FINTRAC notifies you.
- The notification letter requests your program documents and records.
- Reports filed after the notification date are treated as not reported.
- Penalties for violations after March 26, 2026 can be much higher.

### How a FINTRAC examination works

[FINTRAC's assessment manual](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/exam-examen/cam/cams-eng) describes three phases: planning and scoping, examination and assessment, and drawing conclusions and closing out. Examinations can be done remotely (a desk examination) or at your place of business (an on-site examination).

It usually starts with a call to your compliance officer, confirmed in a notification letter. The letter is FINTRAC's formal request for information: your compliance program documents and, where relevant, lists of transactions and records. FINTRAC treats the date it notifies you as the start of the examination.

### Why the notification date matters

A reportable transaction that hasn't been reported by the start of the examination is treated as not reported, and can lead to a finding of failure to submit a report, according to [FINTRAC's examination guidance](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/exam-examen/05-2005/4-eng). Filing it after you've been notified doesn't change that. FINTRAC also says it won't generally accept certain documents or records once an examination has started.

Fix late or missing reports before FINTRAC calls. A regular [effectiveness review](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-effectiveness-review-checklist.html) helps you find them.

### What to do first

- Read the letter carefully and note every deadline. Missing one is itself a risk.

- Gather your compliance program: policies and procedures, risk assessment, training program and records, and your last effectiveness review and its report to a senior officer.

- Pull the records requested, completely and in the format asked for.

- Brief the people involved, especially your compliance officer and anyone FINTRAC may interview.

- Be accurate. Don't create documents after the fact to fill gaps; explain what exists and what you're fixing.

### After the examination

FINTRAC may send a findings letter to your compliance officer, covering the findings discussed at the exit meeting and listing deficient records. The outcome can be no further action, follow-up, a recommended enforcement action, or a notice of violation with a penalty. If an action plan is requested, it's typically due within 30 calendar days.

Administrative monetary penalties aren't automatic. FINTRAC considers the nature and extent of the problem, its root cause, mitigating and aggravating factors, and your compliance history. If you receive a notice of violation, you can make written representations within 30 days. When a penalty is imposed, FINTRAC must make public the name of the person or entity, the nature of the violation and the amount ([PCMLTFA section 73.22](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html)). Past notices are on FINTRAC's [public list of penalties](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/pen/4-eng).

### Changes under Bill C-12

Bill C-12, the Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act, received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. For violations that happen after that date, the maximum penalty is $4 million per violation for a person and $20 million for an entity. A business that receives a penalty must also enter into a compliance agreement with FINTRAC. If it refuses or doesn't comply, FINTRAC's Director must make a compliance order, which is made public.

The amendments also require compliance programs to be reasonably designed, risk-based and effective. Violations that happened entirely before March 26, 2026 stay under the earlier penalty policy. FINTRAC explains the transition on its [penalty changes page](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/pen/3-eng).

### Preparing before FINTRAC calls

- Keep your program current and approved by a senior officer.

- Make sure every reportable transaction has been reported, and late reports are dealt with.

- Keep training records and your last effectiveness review ready to send.

- Close the findings from your last review or examination.

An [outsourced compliance officer](https://amlcanada.ca/outsourced-compliance-officer.html) can help keep these up to date, and an [effectiveness review](https://amlcanada.ca/effectiveness-reviews.html) tests them before FINTRAC does.

### Questions

**How much notice does FINTRAC give before an examination?** FINTRAC's assessment manual says the notification letter usually arrives 30 to 45 days before the examination date, sometimes longer for larger businesses.

**Can FINTRAC examinations be done remotely?** Yes. Examinations can be desk examinations done remotely, or on-site at your place of business.

**Does every deficiency lead to a penalty?** No. FINTRAC says penalties aren't an automatic response. It considers the nature, extent and root cause of the problem and your compliance history.

**What are the maximum FINTRAC penalties now?** For violations after March 26, 2026, up to $4 million per violation for a person and $20 million for an entity, under amendments made by Bill C-12.

Sources: [FINTRAC assessment manual](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/exam-examen/cam/cams-eng); [FINTRAC examinations: what to expect](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/exam-examen/05-2005/4-eng); [Administrative monetary penalties policy](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/pen/2-eng); [Administrative monetary penalties: changes](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/pen/3-eng); [Public notices of penalties](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/pen/4-eng); [FINTRAC, Changes to legislation and regulations](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/businesses-entreprises/changes-changements-eng); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html). Checked 11 October 2026.

---

## Guide: Buying an MSB in Canada: what to check

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/buying-an-msb-canada.html

Buying a company that's already registered with FINTRAC as a money services business needs the same care as any acquisition, plus checks specific to FINTRAC and, for payment businesses, the Bank of Canada.

**Key points:**
- Check the registration on FINTRAC's public registry before you agree a price.
- New owners and managers must not be ineligible under the PCMLTFA.
- Tell FINTRAC about changes, like new owners and directors, within 30 days.
- A PSP registered under the RPAA must re-register before control changes.

### Why some businesses buy

Some businesses acquire a Canadian company that's already registered with FINTRAC as a money services business, instead of [registering a new one](https://amlcanada.ca/how-to-register-msb-canada.html). They start from an established entity with a registration history. It costs more up front, and the due diligence matters as much as the price.

AML Canada sells registered MSBs. Our current companies are listed on [MSB for sale](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-for-sale.html). The checks below apply whichever seller you buy from.

### Check the public registry

Start with [FINTRAC's MSB registry](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/reg-eng). Search by name or registration number and confirm the status is Registered. The other statuses are Revoked, Expired and Ceased. The listing also shows the services the business is registered for, its addresses, and its registration and expiry dates.

Compare the listed services with what you plan to offer. Adding services later means updating the registration. Note the expiry date too: registration lasts two years and must be renewed before it expires. A Registered listing means the business met the legal requirements to register. FINTRAC says it isn't an endorsement.

### Check that the new owners are eligible

Section 11.11 of the [PCMLTFA](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html) makes some persons and entities ineligible to register. They include:

- persons and entities subject to sanctions under the United Nations Act, the Special Economic Measures Act or the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act, or listed under the Criminal Code;

- persons and entities convicted of money laundering, terrorist financing or PCMLTFA offences, or of certain other Criminal Code, drug, customs and tax offences;

- corporations whose director, CEO, president or 20%+ owner has been convicted on indictment of an offence under the PCMLTFA or its predecessor Act;

- since Bill C-12, persons and entities that still haven't paid a FINTRAC penalty, with interest, 30 days after all proceedings on the violation have ended.

If a registered business becomes ineligible, its registration is revoked from that day. If a change of ownership makes the business ineligible, for example under the corporation rule above, the registration you're paying for ends. FINTRAC also needs criminal record checks for the CEO, the president, each director and anyone owning or controlling 20% or more, so plan for these for the incoming people, especially if they live outside Canada.

### Shares or assets

As general information, FINTRAC registration belongs to the registered person or entity. In a share purchase, the company keeps its registration and reports the changes to FINTRAC. If you buy the business's assets into a new or different company, that company needs its own registration before it provides money services.

A share purchase also brings the company's history with it: past transactions, records, any examination findings and any unpaid penalties. Ask your lawyer about warranties and indemnities that cover this.

### What else to check before you buy

- Past FINTRAC examinations, findings letters and action plans, and any published penalties.

- The compliance program, the last two effectiveness reviews and their reports to a senior officer.

- Whether reports were filed on time, and whether records exist for the past five years.

- Corporate records: ownership history, directors, and that the company is in good standing.

- Bank accounts and payment partners, and whether they will continue after the change of control.

### Red flags

- A registry status other than Registered, or an expiry date that has already passed.

- A seller who won't share FINTRAC correspondence or examination results.

- Registered services or transaction estimates that don't match what the business has done.

- No compliance program, or one that was never put into practice.

- Owners or directors who may fall within the ineligibility rules.

### Bank of Canada and Quebec

If the company is also registered with the Bank of Canada as a payment service provider, a planned acquisition of control triggers RPAA section 24. The PSP must submit a new application and be registered again before the acquisition closes. The new application gives the Minister of Finance the chance to carry out a national security review. The [Bank's guidance on acquisitions](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/08/acquisitions-of-control-and-prescribed-changes/) asks PSPs to allow time for both reviews before closing.

In Quebec, money-services businesses also need a licence from [Revenu Québec](https://www.revenuquebec.ca/en/businesses/sector-specific-measures/money-services-businesses-msbs/money-services-business-licence-application/). Revenu Québec decides on a licence only after it receives security clearance reports from the Sûreté du Québec on the business and its associated persons, including directors, officers and anyone who directly or indirectly owns or controls it. New reports are required when a change is likely to affect the licence.

### After the purchase

A registered MSB must tell FINTRAC within 30 days when its registration information changes. A change of ownership usually means several changes at once: owners, directors, senior management, and often the compliance officer and address.

The business still needs a compliance program that reflects its new owners, services and risks, a compliance officer with the authority to do the job, reporting to FINTRAC, record keeping, and renewal every two years. Our [compliance program documents](https://amlcanada.ca/compliance-programs.html) can be rewritten for the new owners. FINTRAC registration also doesn't guarantee banking or payment partners, which make their own decisions.

### Questions

**Can you buy a FINTRAC-registered MSB?** Yes. You can acquire a company that's already registered. Changes to its registration information, such as new owners and directors, must be reported to FINTRAC within 30 days.

**Does the registration transfer if I buy the assets?** As general information, registration belongs to the registered entity. In a share purchase the company keeps it. A new or different company that buys the assets needs its own registration.

**How much does a registered MSB cost?** It varies by company. AML Canada's registered MSBs for acquisition start from €28,000.

**Do new owners need criminal record checks?** Yes. FINTRAC requires criminal record checks for the CEO, the president, each director and anyone owning or controlling 20% or more, so plan for them as part of the purchase.

Sources: [FINTRAC, MSB registry](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/reg-eng); [Register your MSB or FMSB](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/register-inscrire/reg-ins-eng); [Update, renew or cancel your registration](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/register-inscrire/respond-eng); [Money services businesses](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/msb-esm/msb-eng); [Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-24.501/FullText.html); [Bank of Canada, Acquisitions of control](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/08/acquisitions-of-control-and-prescribed-changes/); [Revenu Québec, Money-services business licence](https://www.revenuquebec.ca/en/businesses/sector-specific-measures/money-services-businesses-msbs/money-services-business-licence-application/). Checked 11 October 2026.

## Guide: Outsourced or in-house compliance officer?

URL: https://amlcanada.ca/outsourced-vs-in-house-compliance-officer.html

Every business FINTRAC regulates needs a compliance officer. You can appoint the owner or a manager, hire someone, or outsource the role, and FINTRAC's expectations are the same in each case.

**Key points:**
- Every reporting entity must appoint a compliance officer.
- The officer needs authority and access to resources and decision-makers.
- Small businesses can appoint the owner or operator.
- Your business stays responsible, however the role is filled.

### What FINTRAC expects of a compliance officer

Appointing a compliance officer is the first required element of a compliance program. The person must have the necessary authority and access to resources to implement an effective program, and FINTRAC's best practice is that they can communicate directly with the people who make decisions about the business.

Who it should be depends on size. In a small business, it can be the owner or operator. For a larger business, [FINTRAC's guidance](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/compliance-conformite/Guide4/4-eng) suggests someone from a senior level with direct access to senior management, and says that as a best practice the officer shouldn't be directly involved in receiving, transferring or paying funds.

### Your three options

### 1. Appoint the owner or an existing manager

Common in small businesses. It works when that person has the time and the knowledge. The risk is that compliance competes with everything else they do.

### 2. Hire an in-house compliance officer

Suits larger or fast-growing businesses with steady volumes. You get full-time attention and someone who knows the business from the inside. The costs are a senior salary and the challenge of finding someone experienced with Canadian requirements.

### 3. Use an outsourced compliance officer

An experienced compliance professional carries the day-to-day work, or supports the person you appoint, for the hours you need. They aren't in the business every day, so they rely on the information and access you give them. However it's arranged, your business remains responsible for its obligations, and the arrangement should be set out in writing so it's clear who decides and signs off on what.

### Side by side

| | In-house hire | Outsourced |

| Cost | A full-time salary and benefits, whatever the workload | The hours you use; with us, US$1,500 per 10 hours |

| Presence | In the business every day | Works to an agreed scope and schedule |

| Knowledge of your business | Builds over time from the inside | Depends on what you share and how often |

| Canadian AML experience | Depends on who you can hire | Usually works across several FINTRAC-regulated clients |

| Scaling | Hire more people | Add hours as volumes grow |

| Often suits | Larger businesses with steady volumes | Smaller, new or foreign businesses, or support for an internal officer |

### What the work involves

Whichever option you choose, the work is the same: second-line review of customer onboarding, advice on cases and products, [reporting to FINTRAC](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-reporting-requirements.html) on time, keeping policies and the risk assessment current, client risk ratings, [training](https://amlcanada.ca/training.html), and preparing for the [effectiveness review](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-effectiveness-review-checklist.html) and any [examination](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-examination-preparation.html).

### How to choose

- If no one in the business has AML experience, an outsourced officer can bring it in while you build your own knowledge.

- If you're based outside Canada, consider whether anyone on your team knows Canadian requirements well enough to run the program.

- If volumes are high and steady, an in-house hire, supported by outside reviews, may make sense.

- Some businesses start outsourced and move in-house as they grow.

Our [outsourced compliance officer service](https://amlcanada.ca/outsourced-compliance-officer.html) sets out how the arrangement works with us.

### Questions

**Does every MSB need a compliance officer?** Yes. Appointing a compliance officer is a required part of every reporting entity's compliance program.

**Can a small business owner be the compliance officer?** Yes. FINTRAC's guidance says that in a small business the owner or operator can be the compliance officer.

**How much does an outsourced compliance officer cost?** With us, US$1,500 per block of 10 hours, scaled to your workload.

Sources: [FINTRAC, Compliance program requirements](https://fintrac-canafe.canada.ca/guidance-directives/compliance-conformite/Guide4/4-eng). Checked 11 October 2026.
